## Isaiah 42: verse-by-verse notes

**Overview**
- NET Bible: vv. 1–7 are the first of four "servant songs" (with 49:1–13, 50:4–11 and 52:13–53:12). This song shows the servant as a just king who brings justice to the earth and relief to the oppressed. https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/isa42_notes.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: few deny that the Servant here is the Messiah. The Jewish Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) and the medieval Jewish scholar Abarbanel read it this way, as do Delitzsch and Cheyne. Matthew 12:17–21 applies the passage to Jesus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Matthew Henry: the prophet speaks of the Messiah "under the type of Cyrus" and nearly loses sight of the return from Babylon. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_042.cfm
- Calvin: when the prophets promise something hard to believe, they turn straight to Christ, because every promise is confirmed in Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/42.htm

---

### Part 1: The traditional reading

**v. 1**
- **"Behold" and "Servant":** Guzik says God calls everyone to fix their eyes on His Servant, whom Matthew 12 identifies as Jesus. He adds that Jesus serves His people even now from heaven. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- Pulpit: "Behold" points back to the idols dismissed in ch. 41 and presents the One who replaces them. He is the true, fully obedient Servant, unlike faithless Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- **"Whom I uphold":** Guzik cites Redpath's reading "upon whom I lean," meaning the Father trusts the Son to carry out His purposes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/ Matthew Henry mentions the same reading. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_042.cfm
- Calvin explains "uphold" through the next clause: God will guide Christ by His Spirit and not let difficulties overcome Him. Christ's being a servant was voluntary and takes nothing from His rank (Phil. 2:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/42.htm
- **"Elect" and "delights":** Guzik says believers are chosen "in Him" (Eph. 1:4), and election is an act of love, not cold calculation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/ Ellicott hears this verse echoed in the voice from heaven at Jesus' baptism (Matt. 3:17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- **"My Spirit":** fulfilled at Jesus' baptism (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- **Justice to the nations:** Pulpit says this means making God's true law known to the Gentiles, which the spread of Christianity has fulfilled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- GotQuestions: the baptism voice alludes to Isaiah 42, and the New Testament plainly teaches that Jesus is the Servant. https://www.gotquestions.org/Servant-Songs.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: this doesn't mean Jesus never spoke loudly. It describes His gentle, lowly manner. He quotes Motyer: the Servant does not startle, dominate or advertise himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- Pulpit: His methods are quiet, with no noisy self-promotion. It points to Jesus' many commands not to make Him known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: false prophets might rave, but this teacher has calm authority. The "street" is the open square where speakers addressed crowds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Christ handles our weaknesses tenderly and fans the smoking wick back into flame. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- Pulpit: the reed and wick picture the weak and downcast. Yet "judgment unto truth" means His tenderness never lowers the standard of absolute justice (compare John 8:8–11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: the negative wording implies the opposite, active care. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- Gill: the reed and wick are believers weak in faith and troubled by doubt. He quotes the Targum, which reads them as "the meek" and "the poor." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/42-3.html
- Matthew Henry gives two readings. Christ is tender toward weak believers, and also patient with the wicked, giving them time to repent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/42-3.html
- Calvin: the images do not cover the stubborn and defiant, who must be broken by the word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/42.htm
- Constable: the Servant's calling was to save, not destroy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-42.html
- Spurgeon wrote a devotional on this verse ("Broken and Smoking"). https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-devotionals-c-h-spurgeon

**v. 4**
- Wordplay: the Hebrew words for "fail" and "be discouraged" repeat the words for the dim wick and the bruised reed in v. 3. The Servant has none of the weakness He pities in others (Guzik citing Redpath; Pulpit; Ellicott; MacLaren on the multi-commentary page).
  - https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-3.htm
- **The islands' hope:** Pulpit says the Hebrew means a longing wait. It cites Delitzsch: the cry for redemption runs through the whole human race. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: Matthew 12:21 ("in His name shall the Gentiles hope") follows the Greek Septuagint and is a paraphrase rather than a translation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical commentary applies the verse to Christ persevering to the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: God gives His "credentials" before His promise. Look up (the heavens), look down (the earth), then look at yourself (the breath He gives). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- Pulpit: the prophet starts afresh to make clear that the announcement comes from God Almighty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Matthew Henry: naming God as Creator shows that redemption aims to restore humanity's allegiance to its Maker. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_042.cfm
- Constable: the Servant's work will fulfil the Creator's original purpose for the earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 6**
- Guzik: these are the Father's promises to the Servant (called, held, kept, given), all fulfilled in Jesus. By extension they apply to believers, who are sent as He was (John 17:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- **"A covenant":** Pulpit says Christ embodies the covenant, just as He is called "our Peace." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: He is both the go-between of the covenant and the covenant itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-6.htm
- Constable: the Servant fulfils the covenant for Israel, so the Servant cannot be Israel, or even the faithful remnant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-42.html
- Calvin: as Christ's calling is righteous, God will guard Him as if leading Him by the hand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/42.htm
- Precept Austin's devotional page tells how the hymn-writer Frances Havergal took comfort in this verse on the day she died. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_devotionals_3

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: spiritual blindness is mainly in view, as vv. 16–19 show. The promise is conditional on people being willing to receive it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: the "prison" is selfishness and sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- Coffman: Christ did heal the physically blind, but the real fulfilment is spiritual (compare Luke 4:18). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: if God shares His glory with no one, yet the Son shares the Father's glory (John 17:5), then Father and Son are both the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- Pulpit: the divine name signifies the self-existent, unique God, whose glory cannot be shared, least of all with idols. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Matthew Henry: God is jealous for His name. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_042.cfm

**v. 9**
- **"Former things":** Pulpit says these are earlier prophecies already fulfilled, such as the exile (39:5–7). The "new thing" is a conquering power freely releasing a captive people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: the former things are probably Isaiah's earlier prophecies, or Cyrus's coming conquests. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- Guzik: fulfilled prophecy gives confidence in God's word (2 Pet. 1:19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/

**vv. 10–12**
- Guzik: a psalm-like "new song" from everyone the Servant has touched, including the coastlands. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- Pulpit: the song is new because the mercy is new. It explains the places named:
  - Kedar's "villages" were nomad tent camps.
  - Sela is Petra, the rock-city of Edom.
  - The repeated mention of the "islands" may anticipate Christianity's early successes in the West.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott thinks the call is to the eastern nations, such as ships sailing from Elath. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- Coffman, citing Archer: Gentiles praising God for their conversion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: God goes out as a warrior (compare Exod. 15:3) and wakes His "jealousy," to judge Babylon through Cyrus so that He can free Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: this bold picture prepares for Isaiah 63:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: "long time" is literally "an eternity," though the exile lasted only some decades. This shows how God's love chafed at holding back. The final phrase may be "destroy and devour" (the ancient versions) or "pant and gasp" (most modern scholars). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: the verbs express strong emotion rather than destruction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- Constable: the birth-cry signals a mighty new act. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: the mountains are Babylon's rulers, and drying the rivers may allude to Cyrus diverting rivers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: the picture is symbolic. The rivers and pools likely stand for the Tigris–Euphrates kingdoms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: the blind are captive Israel, led home by an unexpected route, release granted by a new king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- MacLaren (multi-commentary page): stormy judgment serves tender guidance, and the verse foreshadows humanity's greater redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-16.htm
- Spurgeon devotional: "A Sure Guide." https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah-devotionals-c-h-spurgeon

**v. 17**
- Pulpit: the idolatrous oppressors are defeated and put to shame. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: this closes the section, and Cyrus's victories will shame idol-worshippers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- Coffman: salvation comes through judgment and is not for the unrepentant. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: Israel's deafness is chosen, like stopping one's ears (Ps. 58:4). They can hear if they will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Coffman: commanding the deaf to hear shows their inability was wilful. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html

**v. 19**
- NET Bible: the questions mean no one is as blind as this servant. Here the servant is exiled Israel, which failed its calling, in contrast to the ideal servant of the songs. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=isa&chapter=42&verse=19
- Pulpit: Israel was God's original messenger to the nations. "He that is perfect" may mean "he that is rewarded." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: the word means "the surrendered one" and is related to "Muslim." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm
- NET notes that the exact meaning of this word is uncertain. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=isa&chapter=42&verse=19
- GotQuestions: Israel, deaf and blind, failed, while the Messiah completes the mission. https://www.gotquestions.org/Servant-Songs.html
- Guzik: only those who admit they are blind can be healed (John 9:39–41). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: Israel saw much and heard the prophets but did not profit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott: he links this to the scribes and Pharisees of Jesus' day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/42.htm

**v. 21**
- Pulpit translates "it pleased the LORD to magnify the law." This means setting His instruction before Israel through Sinai and the long line of prophets. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Cheyne (quoted by Tuck) reads "to make the instruction great and glorious." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-42.html
- Guzik: God is pleased to honour the law, though under the new covenant we do not come to God on the basis of the law. (The page was cut off after this.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
- A commentator on the Bible Hub v. 22 page: the Lord is pleased to save sinners through Christ's righteousness while also upholding His justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-22.htm

**v. 22**
- Pulpit: despite all God did, Israel sits robbed and trapped in Babylon because of its sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- Ellicott thinks the prophet may foresee a later, more fatal exile, and points to Romans 9–11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-22.htm

**vv. 23–25**
- Guzik: God used this suffering to draw Israel back, only after gentler means had failed, and still Israel did not take it to heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/isaiah/isaiah-42.cfm
- Coffman: even exile did not bring the whole people to repentance, as shown by the few who returned. The picture is of people scorched by fire yet refusing to see their danger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html
- Tuck (Pulpit homilies) calls these "ineffective judgments." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/isaiah-42.html

---

### Part 2: Where interpreters differ

I found no source arguing a denominational position, so these are differences between the commentators I read.

- **v. 3, who the reed and wick are:**
  - Weak believers only (Gill; Calvin explicitly excludes the defiant). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/42-3.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/isaiah/42.htm
  - Weak believers and also the wicked, given time to repent (Matthew Henry). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/42-3.html
- **vv. 1–4 and 13, when it is fulfilled:**
  - Precept Austin's chart puts the full fulfilment of vv. 1–4 in a future Messianic kingdom. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60615/
  - Guzik reads v. 2 against v. 13 as Christ's quiet first coming versus His loud Second Coming. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-42/
  - Pulpit says vv. 13–17 are directly about Cyrus defeating Babylon, and are a picture of the final judgment only in a secondary sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- **v. 6, who "the people" are:**
  - Israel (Ellicott; Delitzsch). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-6.htm
  - Jews and Gentiles together (Barnes, on the same page). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-6.htm
- **v. 16, who the blind are:**
  - Captive Israel (Pulpit). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
  - The Gentiles (Benson), or the Church (Barnes), both on the multi-commentary page. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-16.htm
- **vv. 19–21, which servant:** Pulpit notes that some critics take these verses as being about the Messiah's voluntary humbling. Pulpit rejects that as strained and follows Delitzsch and Cheyne in reading them as about Israel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
- **vv. 22–25, which disaster:**
  - The Babylonian exile (Pulpit). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/42.htm
  - A later exile (Ellicott), or the Roman sack of Jerusalem (another commentator on the Bible Hub page). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-22.htm
  - Coffman applies Israel's hardening "to the present day." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html

---

### Part 3: Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- NET Bible:
  - The servant is pictured as an ideal king, empowered by the Spirit like the king of Isaiah 11.
  - The reed and wick are the oppressed on the edge of extinction.
  - In v. 19 the servant is exiled Israel.
  
  https://bible.org/sites/bible.org/resources/netbible/isa42_notes.htm
- **v. 1, the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation):** it adds "Jacob" and "Israel," which makes the verse refer to the nation (Utley at bible.org). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-42 Bible Hub's parallel-versions page shows that wording too. https://biblehub.com/catholic/isaiah/42-1.htm
- **v. 6:** the Hebrew root behind "keep" is uncertain. It may mean "protect," as in NASB, NKJV and NRSV, or "form," as in NJB and REB (Utley). https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-42
- **Identity of the Servant:** Ellicott sees a "pyramid," with all Israel at the base, the faithful Israel in the middle and the Messiah at the top. Ellicott also refers to "2 Isaiah," the critical view that a second author wrote these chapters. Coffman disputes that view and mentions Duhm, the scholar who first set the servant songs apart.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/42-1.htm
  - https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/isaiah-42.html
- **Early Church writers:** a Bible Hub article says Justin Martyr argued from Isaiah 42 that the Messiah must teach the Gentiles, and that Irenaeus identified the Servant with the Word made flesh. https://biblehub.com/q/Who_is_the_servant_in_Isaiah_42_1.htm

**Catholic Bible wordings (translations only, no commentary)**
- **v. 2:** Douay-Rheims has "nor have respect to person." https://biblehub.com/catholic/isaiah/42-1.htm
- **v. 19:** Douay-Rheims reads "he that is sold" in place of "he that is perfect." https://biblehub.com/isaiah/42-19.htm
- **v. 21:** the Catholic Public Domain Version has "the Lord was willing to sanctify him." https://www.biblehub.com/cpdv/isaiah/42.htm
